Why Synopsys’ Role in AMD’s Instinct MI455X Matters for AI Infrastructureby Daniel Nenni on 10-27-2026 at 8:00 am

View Profile

View Forum Posts

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: EDA, Synopsys

Key takeaways ▼

Synopsys’ collaboration with AMD on the Instinct MI455X GPU highlights a shift in how advanced AI processors are developed. Increasing performance depends on coordinating compute dies, memory interfaces, packaging, power delivery, and software. According to Synopsys’ announcement, AMD used its design, verification, and emulation technologies to manage these connected challenges and accelerate development. The significance extends beyond one accelerator: the collaboration illustrates why integrated engineering tools are becoming essential to the next generation of AI infrastructure.
At the center of the effort was Synopsys’ 3DIC Compiler, which AMD used for multi-die design and advanced package development. The platform supported partitioning, prototyping, floorplanning, automated connections between dies and the package, and integrated physical analysis. Bringing these activities into a shared workflow helped reduce manual work and allowed engineers to evaluate how individual design choices affected the overall system.
This matters because a multi-die accelerator must function as a coordinated whole. Dividing a processor across several dies creates opportunities for architectural flexibility, but it also introduces difficult integration problems. Connections must carry data efficiently, power must reach demanding circuitry, and heat must escape densely packed components. A design that looks effective at the individual die level can encounter bottlenecks once assembled into a complete package.
Synopsys’ integrated multiphysics analysis addressed this interaction between thermal, power, and electromagnetic behavior. These considerations influence one another. Concentrated computation produces heat, while electrical and packaging decisions affect operating conditions and reliability. Evaluating these effects together gives engineers a stronger basis for resolving tradeoffs before manufacturing. The practical value is earlier visibility into problems that could otherwise require expensive changes late in development.
Memory integration was another part of the collaboration. AMD used Synopsys memory interface intellectual property to address the platform’s performance and data movement requirements. For AI accelerators, moving information between memory and compute resources is fundamental to useful performance. Additional computing capacity delivers limited benefit when the surrounding system cannot supply data quickly enough. Memory interfaces therefore belong within the broader architectural discussion, alongside compute capability and packaging.
The collaboration also addressed software readiness through Synopsys’ ZeBu emulation systems. AMD used these systems to validate hardware and develop software before physical silicon became available. Emulation allowed teams to exercise complex workloads, investigate performance bottlenecks, and provide feedback to designers. Synopsys also reported collaboration on emulation models supporting up to 20 billion gates, reflecting the scale of the verification task.
Starting software work earlier matters because an accelerator’s commercial usefulness depends on more than functioning hardware. Drivers, runtime components, and other software must work with the underlying architecture. Discovering integration problems before chips arrive can help teams prepare for bring-up and reduce uncertainty. Save-and-restore capabilities further support debugging by allowing engineers to revisit relevant execution states without repeatedly starting lengthy workloads from the beginning.
AMD additionally used Synopsys’ formal verification, RTL simulation, and low-power verification tools. These approaches provide complementary ways to identify errors and examine behavior across individual dies and the complete system. Their importance grows as architectures become more complex: stronger verification can improve confidence before manufacturing, when correcting a mistake generally becomes more disruptive.
For Synopsys, the announcement demonstrates how its tools span several connected stages of AI chip development. For AMD, it describes an engineering approach intended to support ambitious architectures while managing integration and schedule pressures. For the wider industry, it suggests that development efficiency increasingly depends on connecting disciplines that previously could be handled more independently.
Bottom line:  My takeaway is architectural and operational: as AI accelerators become increasingly interconnected systems, the ability to design, analyze, verify, and prepare software across the entire platform becomes a competitive capability in its own right for chip developers pursuing the next generation of AI infrastructure.
